title: Identify Common Features and Tools of the Linux Client/Desktop Operating System

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Linux technicians often work from the command line. For this objective, recognize the command, configuration file, or operating-system component that fits a stated task.
The main mental model is: files → filesystem → privileges → packages → network → information → configuration → OS components.
bullets: systemd, kernel, bootloader, and the root account

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When a Linux scenario gives you a task, can you identify the correct command, configuration file, or operating-system component?

sections.title: File Management

entries.title: ls
paragraphs: ls lists files and directories.
entries.recognitionCue: See what exists in the current directory → ls.

entries.title: pwd
paragraphs: pwd means print working directory and displays the current filesystem location.
entries.recognitionCue: Display the current directory path → pwd.

entries.title: mv
paragraphs: mv moves a file or directory and can also rename it.
entries.recognitionCue: Rename old.txt to new.txt → mv.

entries.title: cp
paragraphs: cp copies files or directories.
entries.recognitionCue: Create a second copy of a file → cp.

entries.title: rm
paragraphs: rm removes files. Command-line deletion may not provide the easy recovery of a desktop trash or recycle bin.
entries.recognitionCue: Delete a file at the shell → rm.

entries.title: chmod
paragraphs: chmod changes read, write, and execute permissions.
entries.recognitionCue: A script lacks execute permission → chmod.

entries.title: chown
paragraphs: chown changes the owner of a file or directory.
entries.recognitionCue: A file belongs to the wrong user → chown.

entries.title: grep
paragraphs: grep searches text streams or file contents for matching patterns.
entries.recognitionCue: Search a log for the word failed → grep.

entries.title: find
paragraphs: find searches the filesystem for files and directories that match criteria.
entries.recognitionCue: Locate report.txt somewhere under a directory → find.

sections.callout: chmod changes what users can do; chown changes who owns the item. grep finds text; find locates filesystem objects.

entries.title: fsck
paragraphs: fsck checks and can repair filesystem inconsistencies, such as problems following an improper shutdown.
entries.recognitionCue: A Linux filesystem may contain errors → fsck.

entries.title: mount
paragraphs: mount attaches a filesystem to the Linux directory tree at a mount point so its content becomes accessible.
entries.recognitionCue: Make another filesystem accessible at a directory → mount.

sections.title: Administrative

entries.title: su
paragraphs: su switches to another user identity and is commonly associated with switching to root when permitted.

entries.title: sudo
paragraphs: sudo runs an authorized command with elevated privileges without remaining signed in as the superuser.
entries.recognitionCue: Run one package command with administrative authority → sudo.

sections.callout: Switch identity → su. Elevate a specific command → sudo.

sections.title: Package Management
paragraphs: Package managers install, update, and remove software while working with distribution repositories and dependencies.

entries.title: apt
paragraphs: apt is associated with Debian-based distributions, including Ubuntu.
entries.recognitionCue: Install a package on Ubuntu → apt.

entries.title: dnf
paragraphs: dnf is associated with Fedora and related Red Hat-family distributions.
entries.recognitionCue: Install a package on Fedora → dnf.

sections.callout: Debian or Ubuntu → apt. Fedora or RHEL family → dnf.

sections.title: Network

entries.title: ip
paragraphs: The ip command displays and configures network interfaces, addresses, and routes.
entries.recognitionCue: Inspect Linux interface or address information → ip.

entries.title: ping
paragraphs: ping uses ICMP to test basic IP reachability when ICMP is allowed.
entries.recognitionCue: Can the Linux client reach the destination? → ping.

entries.title: curl
paragraphs: curl transfers data to or from URLs and services and is useful for retrieving content or testing an endpoint.
entries.recognitionCue: Test whether a web endpoint returns data → curl.

entries.title: dig
paragraphs: dig queries Domain Name System records and resolver responses.
entries.recognitionCue: Investigate DNS from Linux → dig.

entries.title: traceroute
paragraphs: traceroute displays the network hops toward a destination.
entries.recognitionCue: Show the route traffic takes → traceroute.

sections.callout: ip shows local networking; dig asks DNS; ping checks reachability; traceroute shows the path.

sections.title: Informational

entries.title: man
paragraphs: man displays manual pages containing command descriptions, syntax, and options.
entries.recognitionCue: Need command documentation → man.

entries.title: cat
paragraphs: cat displays file contents and can combine text streams or files.
entries.recognitionCue: Show the contents of /etc/hosts → cat.

entries.title: top
paragraphs: top provides a dynamic, updating view of processes and system-resource use.
entries.recognitionCue: Watch live processes and resource activity → top.

entries.title: ps
paragraphs: ps reports a snapshot or list of process information.
entries.recognitionCue: Capture the current process list → ps.

entries.title: du
paragraphs: du reports space used by files and directories.
entries.recognitionCue: How much space does this folder consume? → du.

entries.title: df
paragraphs: df reports used and available capacity on mounted filesystems.
entries.recognitionCue: How full is this filesystem? → df.

sections.callout: top is live; ps is a snapshot. du measures directory usage; df reports filesystem capacity.

entries.title: nano
paragraphs: nano is a simple terminal-based text editor for files such as configuration documents.
entries.recognitionCue: Edit a text configuration file from the terminal → nano.

sections.title: Common Configuration Files

entries.title: /etc/passwd
paragraphs: Stores user-account information. Modern systems normally store protected password hashes elsewhere.

entries.title: /etc/shadow
paragraphs: Stores restricted password hashes and password-aging information.

entries.title: /etc/hosts
paragraphs: Stores local static hostname-to-IP mappings for the individual system.
entries.recognitionCue: Manually map one hostname locally → /etc/hosts.

entries.title: /etc/fstab
paragraphs: Defines filesystems, mount points, and mount options used for persistent or automatic mounting.
entries.recognitionCue: Configure a filesystem to mount at boot → /etc/fstab.

entries.title: /etc/resolv.conf
paragraphs: Contains DNS resolver configuration on many Linux systems.
entries.recognitionCue: Identify configured DNS resolver information → /etc/resolv.conf.

sections.callout: /etc/hosts supplies local mappings; /etc/resolv.conf defines resolver behavior.

entries.title: systemd
paragraphs: systemd is a common system and service manager that initializes and manages Linux services.

entries.title: Kernel
paragraphs: The kernel is the OS core that manages CPU, memory, processes, hardware, and the interface between software and hardware.

entries.title: Bootloader
paragraphs: The bootloader begins the operating-system startup process and loads the kernel.

sections.title: Root Account
paragraphs: The root account is the Linux superuser with extensive system-wide authority. Use it carefully; when appropriate, administrators use sudo for individual elevated commands rather than remaining logged in as root.
sections.callout: Root is the superuser; sudo limits elevation to an authorized command.

entries.title: chmod vs. chown
paragraphs: chmod changes permissions; chown changes ownership.

entries.title: grep vs. find
paragraphs: grep searches text content; find locates files and directories.

entries.title: su vs. sudo
paragraphs: su switches identity; sudo elevates a command.

entries.title: apt vs. dnf
paragraphs: apt belongs to Debian/Ubuntu families; dnf belongs to Fedora/Red Hat families.

entries.title: top vs. ps
paragraphs: top is a dynamic live view; ps is a process snapshot.

entries.title: du vs. df
paragraphs: du reports directory or file usage; df reports filesystem capacity and free space.

entries.title: /etc/passwd vs. /etc/shadow
paragraphs: passwd stores account information; shadow stores protected password data.

entries.title: /etc/hosts vs. /etc/resolv.conf
paragraphs: hosts supplies local mappings; resolv.conf configures DNS resolution.
